title: Prove Orbit as the durable terminal runtime beneath Mars
description: Determine whether a small Rust and libghostty runtime can replace the PTY and session-lifetime role that Zellij provides beneath Mars. The authorized experiment is Linux-only, local, one-session, and one-active-client. Either a go or no-go result completes the architectural experiment.
design: docs/RATIONALE.md records the origin, ownership hypothesis, prior art, tradeoffs, and stop criteria. Mars and Mars Next remain behavioral references. The epic excludes multiplayer, remote transport, Zellij compatibility, layouts, tabs, plugins, a configuration framework, daemon-restart persistence, and unapproved libghostty forks or wrappers. Bead evidence may narrow the plan but cannot widen it without a user decision.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Every required experiment or decision bead closes with reproducible evidence.
2. orb-bi4.8 records an explicit user go or no-go decision.
3. On a go decision, orb-bi4.7 records accepted, rejected, or deferred ownership boundaries before promotion planning. On a no-go decision, orb-bi4.7 closes as not applicable.
4. No known P0 or P1 correctness risk remains unrecorded.
5. The README LOC scorecard and rationale match the final experimental state.

title: Prove the libghostty attachment model
description: Answer the highest-risk question before building runtime architecture: can the released libghostty-vt Rust API support one headless authoritative terminal and reconstruct a second terminal that continues correctly from an ordered PTY tail?
design: Use the current released libghostty-vt crate and record the exact version and source. Compare the smallest viable attachment strategies: direct state export and import if available; a VT bootstrap derived from public formatting and state APIs; or a bounded checkpoint plus raw replay. Reject unbounded history replay. Account for the library unstable API, single-thread ownership of !Send and !Sync terminal objects, terminal-generated PTY responses, and the boundary between semantic input events and encoded bytes. Only Orbit may answer terminal queries back to the PTY. Test hidden state that can alter future bytes: cursor and keyboard modes, pending wrap, alternate screen, tab stops, character sets, palette and hyperlinks, scrollback where required for future resize, and a parser between escape-sequence bytes. Stop for a user decision before adding a fork, compatibility layer, or substantial wrapper.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A minimal Linux Rust proof builds against a recorded released libghostty-vt version with the real feature enabled by default.
2. The proof feeds deterministic VT input into authoritative state and reconstructs a second terminal using the most promising public-API strategy.
3. A distinguishing future tail produces equivalent semantic behavior, including hidden modes rather than only equal visible cells.
4. The result states which screen, scrollback, mode, parser, effect, input-encoding, palette, hyperlink, and image state the strategy preserves or loses.
5. The result records thread ownership, required callbacks, dependency footprint, and Rust LOC.
6. Failure identifies the missing API and a reproducible counterexample; it does not introduce a fork or unbounded replay.
notes: Prime audit evidence, 2026-08-03: docs.rs lists libghostty-vt 0.2.1, released 2026-07-18, and warns that the API is unstable. Terminal owns full emulator state, while RenderState describes the visible viewport needed to draw a frame. The Rust handles are documented as !Send and !Sync and should remain on one owner thread with channel communication. The formatting API can emit VT for selections, but the 0.2.1 public documentation does not advertise full terminal-state serialization or import. Recheck the release and source when claiming this bead rather than treating this planning observation as final API truth. References: https://docs.rs/crate/libghostty-vt/0.2.1 and https://docs.rs/libghostty-vt/latest/libghostty_vt/

title: Prove PTY lifetime across diagnostic-client disconnect
description: Build the smallest headless Orbit vertical slice that proves process persistence and local transport. Orbit owns one real PTY shell and one libghostty terminal on a single owner thread. One diagnostic client connects over a local Unix socket. Exact terminal reconstruction remains the outcome of orb-bi4.3.
design: Keep one Rust package and binary unless evidence establishes another owner. Use the attachment strategy and thread model accepted in orb-bi4.1. Keep the server in the foreground for the experiment; daemonization policy is deferred. Use a minimal bounded message set rather than a general protocol framework. Orbit owns terminal-generated PTY writes. Decide and record whether the client sends semantic key, mouse, focus, and paste events for server-side encoding or sends encoded bytes; raw bytes are acceptable only if they preserve authoritative mode behavior. The active client controls PTY size, and the server retains the last size while detached. Place the socket in a user-private runtime location and define stale-socket cleanup.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A subprocess check starts a real shell, attaches a diagnostic client, exchanges input and output, and changes PTY size.
2. Client disconnect leaves the shell and foreground process alive; output produced while detached reaches authoritative server state.
3. A later diagnostic connection reaches the same live PTY. This is a lifecycle smoke test, not convergence proof.
4. A second simultaneous attach receives one deterministic rejection without disturbing the active client.
5. Child exit, server shutdown, signal handling, process reaping, socket permissions, and stale-socket cleanup have explicit checked behavior.
6. Checks use observable synchronization and bounded timeouts rather than sleep as a correctness mechanism.

title: Implement and prove atomic terminal convergence on reattach
description: Implement the defining Orbit contract on the real PTY slice: a client attaches at one atomic boundary, receives a coherent terminal bootstrap, then receives every later PTY byte once and in order until disconnect.
design: Use the public-API attachment strategy accepted in orb-bi4.1. Serialize PTY reads, authoritative libghostty writes, snapshot creation, and tail subscription through one owner so there is no race window. The reconstructed client must suppress PTY-directed effects during bootstrap and tail replay; Orbit remains the only terminal-query responder. Use authoritative semantic state plus future distinguishing input as the oracle. Either transfer parser-in-progress state or prove a parser-stable boundary with lossless buffering. Separate user-visible scrollback navigation from any history state required for semantic convergence.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A real PTY establishes terminal state, emits output during detachment, and continues output while a new client attaches.
2. Tests detect missing, duplicated, or reordered bytes across the bootstrap-to-tail boundary.
3. A corpus covers hidden modes, pending wrap, alternate screen, palette or hyperlink state, Unicode, and an escape sequence split at the attach boundary.
4. Varying PTY read chunk boundaries does not change the reconstructed result.
5. A future distinguishing tail makes server and client produce equivalent semantic and visible state.
6. Tests use explicit barriers and bounded timeouts, retain no weak screenshot-only checks, and fail reproducibly if the contract cannot be met.

title: Render the proven Orbit session in one native Linux window
description: Add the smallest graphical client needed to dogfood the proven session contract: one Linux window that renders client-side libghostty-vt state and sends input and resize events to the existing Orbit session.
design: Propose the windowing, font, and rendering dependencies with an owned-LOC estimate for user approval before adding them. Use libghostty-vt RenderState as the terminal model and do not introduce a second terminal-semantics implementation. Follow the input boundary decided in orb-bi4.2. Keep Orbit as the experiment name; Mars naming waits for graduation. Exclude tabs, panes, settings UI, decorations, frosted glass, configuration, shell integration, compatibility work, and general UI architecture.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The client builds and opens one Linux window attached to an already running Orbit session.
2. It renders styled text, Unicode, cursor state, and a full-screen alternate-screen application from reconstructed client state.
3. Keyboard input and resize reach the PTY through the chosen authoritative boundary.
4. Closing or crashing the window leaves the PTY alive; reopening reconstructs and resumes the session.
5. Attach rejection and server loss produce clear bounded failures rather than hangs.
6. Focused nonvisual checks cover deterministic rendering inputs; manual window dogfood records the remaining visual evidence.

title: Harden the one-client attachment boundary
description: Challenge the proven client and server at the transport, terminal-semantics, and process-lifecycle boundaries most likely to invalidate the architecture. This bead hardens the chosen contract and adds no product features.
design: Keep buffers and frames bounded. Exercise rapid output, a client that stops reading, EOF during a frame, client crash, attach races, and a second attach. Exercise alternate screen, Unicode and combining characters, partial escape sequences, terminal-query responses, and resize while attached or detached. Exercise PTY exit, server shutdown, signals, and socket cleanup. Do not expand into multiplayer, remote transport, daemon restart recovery, image support, or general protocol extensibility.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Focused checks or reproducible dogfood define behavior for every listed transport, terminal, and lifecycle boundary.
2. Rapid output and attach races produce no byte gap, duplication, reordering, deadlock, or unbounded memory growth.
3. A slow or failed client cannot block authoritative PTY processing indefinitely.
4. Terminal-generated responses reach the PTY once, including during bootstrap and reattach.
5. Invalid or truncated local frames, process exits, and signals fail clearly and clean up owned resources.
6. Checks use explicit synchronization and bounded timeouts; redundant or implementation-trivia tests are removed.

title: Dogfood Orbit through an opt-in Yazelix path
description: Package the proven Orbit revision in Yazelix Nova behind an explicit opt-in path while preserving the current Mars and Zellij runtime as the default. Use fresh-session dogfood to compare the experiment with the current chain.
design: Make integration changes on the Yazelix edge branch and pin the exact Orbit revision in the Nix flake. Do not broaden Home Manager, layouts, config generation, plugins, pane policy, or compatibility. Keep normal yzx behavior unchanged. Update Yazelix README, CHANGELOG, and LOC scorecard for the opt-in command. Refresh the installed runtime after the flake changes. Record friction and failures in this bead instead of widening Orbit during dogfood.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The approved opt-in command launches the pinned Orbit revision in a fresh session, while normal yzx still launches the current Mars and Zellij chain.
2. nix flake check, nix flake show --all-systems, nix build .#yazelix --no-link --print-build-logs, and installation into a temporary profile pass in Yazelix.
3. The user installed profile is refreshed from the Yazelix checkout after the runtime change.
4. Fresh-session dogfood covers a shell, Neovim, Yazi, a full-screen TUI, and a long-running process across client detach and reattach.
5. Record comparable startup, high-output, idle-memory, and interaction observations against the current Zellij path; make no performance claim without evidence.
6. Documentation describes the opt-in path as experimental and leaves promotion or retirement decisions to later beads.

title: Choose post-graduation Orbit ownership boundaries
description: After a go decision in orb-bi4.8, ask the user which responsibilities Orbit should own beyond the proven one-session contract. On a no-go decision, close this bead as not applicable.
design: Treat each option as a separate scope choice: multiple independent sessions while retaining one active client per session; user-visible scrollback and history navigation beyond state required for convergence; pane or workspace topology; Orbit restart recovery; shell integration; and richer terminal protocols. For each option, record observed user need, one proposed owner, the cheapest proving check, expected owned LOC, maintenance cost, and accept, reject, or defer. Do not create implementation beads before the user accepts an option. Multiplayer remains excluded.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The orb-bi4.8 graduation decision is recorded first.
2. After a go, every listed responsibility has an explicit accept, reject, or defer decision from the user.
3. Accepted responsibilities identify one owner and may receive implementation beads only after that decision.
4. Rejected alternatives and reasons remain in this bead.
5. After a no-go, the bead closes as not applicable without speculative planning.

title: Decide whether Orbit earns graduation beneath Mars
description: Make the explicit go or no-go decision after the core contract, native client, hardening, and fresh Yazelix dogfood are complete. This decision evaluates the narrow experiment before any optional ownership expansion.
design: Compare Orbit with the current Mars and Zellij path and with continuing Mars Next. Evaluate correctness, user-visible coherence, project-owned LOC, dependency and upgrade burden, measured performance, and Zellij workflows lost by the narrow scope. A go authorizes the architectural direction and unblocks orb-bi4.7; it does not authorize replacing the current default, removing Zellij, renaming the client to Mars, or promoting channels. A no-go records what evidence or code should be retained or deleted. Create follow-up implementation or cleanup beads only after the user chooses them.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Summarize attachment and lifecycle evidence, known limitations, actual Rust LOC, dependency footprint, maintenance risks, dogfood results, measured performance observations, lost Zellij functionality, and all remaining P0 or P1 risks.
2. State whether Orbit is materially simpler and more coherent for Yazelix than the current alternatives.
3. Obtain and record an explicit user go or no-go decision.
4. On go, unblock the ownership decisions in orb-bi4.7 without changing the default runtime.
5. On no-go, record the retain or delete choice and close orb-bi4.7 as not applicable.
6. Create no promotion, retirement, rename, or cleanup bead without the corresponding user choice.
